title: Cadence Trellis: micro-burst cadence experiments (scratch)
content:
Goal:
- Quick exploration of rhythmic arrival patterns (non-Poisson), here called "trellis cadence". See whether short periodic microbursts + quiet windows can be smoothed by: (A) lightweight prefetch primes, (B) micro-coalescing window, (C) KV-cache priming policy.

Context / why: 
- Prod saw multidimensional tail amplifications when a small subset of tenants send tightly-clustered requests (20–100 reqs in <200ms windows).
- Hypothesis: a small, controlled priming signal before a burst can (1) reduce p99 by avoiding cold KV misses and kernel startups, (2) allow batching without delaying p50.

Setup (short):
- Model: llm-6b-quant (int8-w/kv-compat), sequence length 256 average.
- Hardware: 8xA100 (dedicated pool) but experiments limited to a single GPU endpoint simulating multi-tenant mix.
- Runtime flags: continuous-batching=true, coalesce-window=10ms/20ms/50ms, prefetch=on/off/heuristic, kv-cache-ttl=30s/120s/inf.
- Client arrival generator: deterministic trellis waveform (sine-modulated Poisson) + repeatable seed. Burst groups: 16/48/128 reqs per burst.
- Measuring: p50/p90/p95/p99, tail amplification factor (p99 / p50), batch size distribution, KV cache hit-rate, token cost. 10 runs per config, 95% CI.

Quick notes on cmds used:
- workload generator: bench/trellis-gen --rate 60 --burst-size 48 --burst-interval 800ms --jitter 5% --seed 20241114
- endpoint: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' "https://redwood.local/v1/generate?model=llm-6b-quant" --data-binary @payload.json

Key runs & results (condensed):
1) baseline (no-prefetch, coalesce=10ms, kv-ttl=30s)
   - p50 38ms, p90 95ms, p95 132ms, p99 420ms (tail amplification 11x)
   - batch size median 1, mean 2.1, 70% singletons during bursts
   - kv-hit 0.21 during initial bursts, warms to 0.65 after ~12s

2) prefetch pulse (tiny prime 8 tokens 50ms before predicted burst)
   - p50 40ms (noop), p90 88ms, p95 120ms, p99 210ms (tail amp 5.2x)
   - kv-hit jumps to 0.62 at burst start; batch size median 2, mean 3.8
   - token cost +3.6%, but tail latency cut ~50%

3) micro-coalesce=50ms (no prefetch)
   - p50 44ms, p90 80ms, p95 110ms, p99 260ms (tail amp 6x)
   - batching reduces singletons to 22% during burst; some p50 regressions due to wait window for earliest requests

4) combined (prefetch + micro-coalesce 20ms + kv-ttl=120s)
   - p50 42ms, p90 76ms, p95 102ms, p99 150ms (tail amp 3.6x)
   - kv-hit steady 0.82; sustained throughput improved ~18% effective tokens/sec
   - token cost +4.8% vs baseline; p99 improved ~64%

5) stress (burst-size 128, coalesce 50ms, prefetch heuristic=aggressive)
   - p99 360ms; observed periodic kernel thrash at ~every 9th burst (suspect GPU kernel scheduling + memory churn)

Observations / interpretation:
- Small prefetch primes are highly cost-effective when bursts are predictable (scheduled or follow rhythmic patterns). A tiny steady priming cost pays off for tail improvements.
- Micro-coalescing windows reduce tail but introduce small p50 regressions. For user-facing low-latency flows, aim for 10–25ms coalesce; for batch-y flows, 50ms is fine.
- KV-ttl matters: making TTL longer for tenants with periodic spikes prevents cold miss cascades. But long TTL increases memory pressure in dense multi-tenant hosts; need eviction policy integration.
- Combined approach (prefetch + short coalesce + slightly raised kv-ttl) gave best tradeoff in these synthetic trellis patterns.
- Stress runs show emergent kernel-level thrash under extreme bursts; likely due to GPU memory allocation/free churn and attention-kernel selection oscillation. Need lower-level profiling (nvprof + internal kernel traces).

Quick heuristics for rollout (for engineering):
- If burst predictability score > 0.6 (from ingress classifier), enable prefetch pulse 50ms before predicted cluster.
- Default coalesce window 15ms for interactive tiers; allow 30–50ms for throughput tiers.
- Use tenant-local KV-ttl of 90–120s for rhythm-detected tenants; gate by memory quota.

Open questions & next steps:
- Can we automate optimal prefetch size per-model (token count) based on historical cold-miss cost? (A/B candidate: 4 vs 8 vs 12 tokens)
- Add kernel-level tracing during stress to confirm memory churn hypothesis. Link to perf PR: GHE PR 812 (see linked_artifacts).
- Run real-client blended replay (sampling from prod traces) to validate synthetic trellis assumptions.
- Explore adaptive coalesce: start with 10ms, if burst density > threshold expand to 30ms mid-burst, then shrink after burst end. Need low-latency feedback (socket-level).

Notes-to-self:
- Plot p99 vs coalesce-window for different burst sizes (visual shows elbow around 25–30ms).
- Run with quantized int4 variant; integer kernels may change kernel-swap patterns.
- Keep an eye on cost-per-token vs tail-reduction metric — define a combined objective for rollout decisions (e.g., tail-reduction-per-0.1% cost increase).

Summary (one-liner):
- For rhythmic microbursts, tiny priming pulses + short coalescing windows + moderate KV-ttl yield large p99 wins for modest token cost increases; extreme bursts still need kernel/driver-level investigation.

Raw measurement snippets (single-run example):
- run_id: trellis-20241114-01
- config: coalesce=20ms, prefetch=8t@50ms, kv-ttl=120s
- p50,p90,p95,p99: 42,76,102,150
- batches: [1,1,2,3,5,1,2,3,10,2,...] (median 2)
- kv-hit timeline: 0.18->0.61@burst-start->0.82 steady

End of scratch pad — will formalize into a short runbook and propose a safe canary for interactive tier.
